decks.title: Relations and Functions - Part 1: Cartesian products, relations and functions
goals: Write the Cartesian product of two finite sets and state its size
Find the number of relations from one finite set to another
Show a relation by an arrow diagram and state its domain, co-domain and range
Decide whether a relation is a function and justify the answer

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 1
slides.body_md: From pairs of objects to rules that give exactly one answer.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: ordered pairs, the Cartesian product, counting pairs and relations, relations with arrow diagrams, and functions as special relations.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on relations and functions. A shop list matches items to prices, a timetable matches days to subjects, and a roll list matches students to numbers. In this part you will learn to describe such matches precisely with ordered pairs, and to decide when a match is a function.

slides.heading: Ordered pairs
slides.body_md: An **ordered pair** $(a, b)$ has a first entry and a second entry; $(a, b) = (c, d)$ exactly when $a = c$ and $b = d$.

rows: Yes: same entries in the same places

visual.alt: Table comparing ordered pairs: the pairs (2, 7) and (7, 2) are different, (5, 5) equals (5, 5), and two general pairs are equal only when the first entries agree and the second entries agree.
visual.caption: An ordered pair remembers which entry comes first.

slides.narration: An ordered pair keeps its entries in order. The pair two, seven is not the same as the pair seven, two, because the first entries differ. Two pairs are equal only when the first entries agree and the second entries agree. This is different from a set, where order does not matter.

slides.heading: Pairs as points in the plane
slides.body_md: The pair $(2, 4)$ and the pair $(4, 2)$ give two different points, mirror images in the line $y = x$.

visual.alt: Coordinate plane with the line y equals x. The points (2, 4) and (4, 2) are mirror images in this line, so they are two different points, just as the ordered pairs are different.
visual.caption: $(2, 4) \ne (4, 2)$: swapping the entries moves the point.

slides.narration: Every ordered pair of real numbers is a point in the coordinate plane. The pairs two, four and four, two sit at different places, mirror images in the line where y equals x. That is why we say the pair is ordered: swapping the entries moves the point.

slides.heading: The Cartesian product
slides.body_md: $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$. For infinite sets, $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is the plane and $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is space.

visual.alt: Grid for the product of A equal to the set 1, 2, 3 and B equal to the set p, q: the six ordered pairs (1, p), (1, q), (2, p), (2, q), (3, p), (3, q), one in each row and column cell.
visual.caption: Rows run over $A$, columns over $B$: $3 \times 2 = 6$ pairs.

slides.narration: The Cartesian product of A and B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first entry comes from A and whose second entry comes from B. Think of a grid: rows run over A, columns run over B, and each cell is one pair. With the real numbers, the product of R with R is the whole plane, and three copies give space.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: A times B and B times A
slides.body_md: Let $A = \{4, 7\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 3\}$. Write $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ and compare them.
bullets: Both have $6$ pairs, but $(4, 3)$ is only in $A \times B$

rows: No: $(4, 3) \in A \times B$ but $(4, 3) \notin B \times A$

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: for A equal to 4, 7 and B equal to 1, 2, 3, the product A times B and the product B times A each have 6 pairs, but the two sets are different, for instance (4, 3) is in the first and not in the second.
visual.caption: Same number of pairs, different pairs.

slides.narration: Pair each element of the first set with every element of the second. The first product has six pairs, and so does the second. But the pair four, three appears in the first product and not in the second. So the two products have the same number of pairs, yet they are different sets.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal pairs
slides.body_md: Decide when two ordered pairs with swapped entries are equal.
slides.narration: Compare the first entries and the second entries separately, and see what that forces.

slides.heading: Counting pairs and relations
slides.body_md: $n(A \times B) = n(A)\,n(B)$ and $n(A \times B \times C) = n(A)\,n(B)\,n(C)$. A relation is any **subset** of $A \times B$, so there are $2^{pq}$ relations.

visual.alt: Counting table: for set sizes 2 and 3 the product has 6 pairs and there are 64 relations; for 3 and 3 there are 9 pairs and 512 relations; for 4 and 5 there are 20 pairs and 1048576 relations.
visual.caption: Pairs multiply; relations are subsets of the pairs, so they count as $2^{pq}$.

slides.narration: Counting is multiplication. If A has p elements and B has q elements, the product has p times q pairs. Every subset of the product is a relation from A to B, including the empty set and the whole product. A set with p q elements has two to the power p q subsets, so that many relations exist.

slides.heading: Quick check: triples
slides.body_md: Count the ordered triples in a product of three finite sets.
slides.narration: Choose the three entries one after another and multiply the number of choices.

slides.heading: Relations: domain, co-domain and range
slides.body_md: A **relation** $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A \times B$. Domain: first entries used. Co-domain: the set $B$. Range: second entries used.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from A equal to 1, 2, 3, 4 to B equal to 0, 3, 8, 10, 15: the arrows go 1 to 0, 2 to 3, 3 to 8 and 4 to 15, so 10 receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $y = x^2 - 1$: domain $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, range $\{0, 3, 8, 15\}$, co-domain all of $B$.

slides.narration: An arrow diagram draws each pair as an arrow from the first set to the second. Here the rule is y equals x squared minus one. The domain is the set of elements that start an arrow. The range is the set of elements that receive an arrow. The co-domain is the whole second set, and it may contain elements, like ten, that no arrow reaches.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a relation from a rule
slides.body_md: From $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ to $B = \{2, 3, 4, 5\}$ let $x\,R\,y$ mean $x + y = 7$. List $R$ and find its domain and range.
bullets: Domain $= \{2, 3, 4, 5\}$ (the elements $1$ and $6$ have no partner in $B$)

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of the relation x plus y equal to 7 from A equal to 1 to 6 to B equal to 2 to 5: 2 goes to 5, 3 goes to 4, 4 goes to 3 and 5 goes to 2, while 1 and 6 have no arrow.
visual.caption: Elements $1$ and $6$ of $A$ have no partner, so they are outside the domain.

slides.narration: Test every element of the first set. For one, the partner would be six, which is not in B, so one has no arrow. For two, the partner is five, for three it is four, for four it is three and for five it is two. Six would need one, which is not in B. So there are four pairs, and domain and range are both two to five.

slides.heading: Quick check: how many relations
slides.body_md: Count the relations from a three-element set to a one-element set.
slides.narration: First count the pairs in the product, then count the subsets.

slides.heading: Quick check: a big count
slides.body_md: Test the counting rule for relations on a product with twelve pairs.
slides.narration: Every pair is either in the relation or out of it.

slides.heading: Functions as special relations
slides.body_md: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a **function** when every element of $A$ has **exactly one** image in $B$. We write $y = f(x)$.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a function from X equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1, 2 to Y equal to 1, 4, 9: each element of X has exactly one arrow, minus 2 and 2 both go to 4, minus 1 and 1 both go to 1, and 9 receives none.
visual.caption: One arrow from every element of $X$; two elements may share an image.

slides.narration: A function is a relation with a strict rule: every element of the first set must have exactly one arrow leaving it. Here each element of X has one arrow. Two elements may arrive at the same image, so minus two and two both map to four. And the second set may have unused elements, like nine. The range is only the set of images reached.

slides.heading: When a relation fails to be a function
slides.body_md: Two things break the rule: an element with **two** images, or an element with **no** image.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation that is not a function: from X equal to 1, 2, 3 to Y equal to 4, 5, 6, the element 1 has two arrows, to 4 and to 5, and the element 3 has no arrow at all.
visual.caption: $1$ has two images and $3$ has none: not a function.

slides.narration: Here the element one has two arrows, to four and to five, so it has two images. The element three has no arrow at all. Either failure is enough to stop this relation from being a function. Remember, it is fine for two inputs to share an output, but never for one input to have two outputs.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing element
slides.body_md: Decide whether an element with no partner can be allowed in a function.
slides.narration: Think about what every element of the first set must have.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: function or not?
slides.body_md: Which of the three relations from $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{7, 8\}$ are functions?
bullets: Check every element of $\{1, 2, 3\}$ for exactly one image
The second leaves $3$ out; the third gives $1$ two images

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: of three relations from 1, 2, 3 to 7, 8, only the first is a function; the second leaves 3 without an image and the third gives 1 two images.
visual.caption: Every element of the domain set needs exactly one image.

slides.narration: For each relation, go through the elements one, two and three. In the first relation each has exactly one image, so it is a function. In the second, three has no image. In the third, one has two images, seven and eight. So only the first relation is a function, and each verdict needs its reason.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Domain, co-domain, range of a relation
Function: exactly one image for every element of $A$

nodes.label: Relation: a subset of $A \times B$; $2^{pq}$ of them
Function: exactly one image for each element

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: ordered pairs where order matters, the Cartesian product with p times q pairs, a relation as any subset of the product with 2 to the power pq choices, and a function as a relation with exactly one image for every element.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. An ordered pair keeps its order. The product of two sets with p and q elements has p times q pairs, and a relation is any subset of the product. The domain is the set of first entries, the range is the set of second entries. A function gives every element of the first set exactly one image.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: List pairs **in order**, row by row
Do not confuse range with co-domain
Justify yes or no for a function **with a reason**

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: test applied 1, reason for the verdict 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: listing a product earns method and list marks, counting questions earn the rule and the number, rule-based relations earn the pairs plus domain and range, and function questions earn the test and the reason.
visual.caption: Always give a reason when you say yes or no.

slides.narration: In the examination, list the pairs in a tidy order so that none is missed. Do not confuse the range with the co-domain. When you say a relation is or is not a function, always give the reason, naming the element with no image or with two images. And count relations with two to the power p q, not p plus q.

decks.title: Relations and Functions - Part 2: Real functions, standard graphs and algebra of functions
goals: Find the domain and range of a real function
Sketch the modulus, signum and greatest integer functions
State the domain and range of the standard real functions from their graphs
Find f + g, f - g, fg and f / g with their domains

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 2
slides.body_md: Which inputs are allowed, which outputs appear, and how functions combine.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the domain of a real function, the range found by solving for x, the standard functions with their graphs, and the algebra of real functions.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A real function takes real numbers in and gives real numbers out, but not every input is allowed. In this part you will find which inputs work, which outputs appear, learn the graphs of the standard functions, and combine functions by adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing.

slides.heading: Domain of a real function
slides.body_md: When a real function is given only by a formula, its domain is the **largest set** of real numbers for which the formula gives a real value.

visual.alt: Table of domain rules for real functions: a fraction needs a non-zero denominator, an even root needs a non-negative quantity, a root in a denominator needs a positive quantity, and a logarithm needs a positive argument.
visual.caption: Test each part of the rule, then combine the conditions.

slides.narration: To find a domain, ask what could go wrong. A fraction fails when its denominator is zero. An even root fails when the quantity inside is negative. A logarithm fails unless its argument is positive. Test each part of the rule, write the condition it forces, then keep only the numbers that satisfy all conditions together.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a root over a linear factor
slides.body_md: Find the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 3}}{x - 1}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: for the function square root of x plus 3 over x minus 1, the root needs x at least minus 3, the denominator needs x not equal to 1, and together the domain is all x from minus 3 upwards except 1.
visual.caption: Intersect the two conditions.

slides.narration: Two things can go wrong here. The root needs the quantity inside to be zero or more, so x must be at least minus three. The denominator must not be zero, so x cannot be one. Combine both conditions: all numbers from minus three upwards, with one removed. Note that minus three is allowed, because the root of zero is fine.

slides.heading: Quick check: a smallest integer
slides.body_md: Find the smallest integer in the domain of a square root function.
slides.narration: Solve the root condition, then pick the first whole number that satisfies it.

slides.heading: Range by solving for x
slides.body_md: Put $y = f(x)$ and solve for $x$. The values of $y$ for which a real $x$ in the domain exists form the **range**.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal to 3 minus 2x over x plus 4: two branches either side of the vertical line x equal to minus 4. The right branch crosses the x-axis at 1.5 and flattens towards the height minus 2; the left branch lies below minus 2.
visual.caption: Solving for $x$ gives $x = \dfrac{3 - 4y}{y + 2}$: every $y$ except $-2$ is a value.

slides.narration: To find a range, set y equal to the rule and solve for x. If the solution exists as a real number in the domain, that y is a value of the function. Here we reach x equals three minus four y over y plus two, which fails only when y is minus two. So the range is all real numbers except minus two, matching the graph, which flattens towards that height.

slides.heading: Quick check: a range
slides.body_md: Decide whether the values of a quadratic fill a stated interval.
slides.narration: Complete the square to find the smallest value, then ask whether every larger value occurs.

slides.heading: Standard real functions
slides.body_md: Constant, identity, polynomial, rational, modulus, signum, greatest integer, exponential and logarithmic functions are the building blocks.

visual.alt: Table of the standard real functions with their domain and range: constant, identity, square, reciprocal, modulus, signum, greatest integer, exponential and logarithmic.
visual.caption: Learn the domain and range with each graph.

slides.narration: Here are the standard functions with their domains and ranges. The constant function has a single value. The identity and every polynomial are defined everywhere. The reciprocal misses zero. The modulus is never negative. The signum has only three values. The greatest integer gives whole numbers. The exponential is always positive, and the logarithm is defined only for positive inputs.

slides.heading: The modulus function
slides.body_md: $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ for $x < 0$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal to mod x: a V shape with its tip at the origin, passing through (minus 3, 3) and (2, 2), lying on or above the x-axis everywhere.
visual.caption: $|x| \ge 0$: range $[0, \infty)$, symmetric about the $y$-axis.

slides.narration: The modulus function gives the distance from zero. For positive x it is x itself, and for negative x it is minus x. The graph is a V with its tip at the origin. It never goes below the horizontal axis, so the range is zero upwards, and it is symmetric about the vertical axis.

slides.heading: The signum function
slides.body_md: $\operatorname{sgn}(x) = 1$ for $x > 0$, $0$ for $x = 0$, $-1$ for $x < 0$.

visual.alt: Graph of the signum function: a horizontal ray at height minus 1 to the left of the origin, a horizontal ray at height 1 to the right, and the single point (0, 0) between them.
visual.caption: Only three values: $-1$, $0$ and $1$.

slides.narration: The signum function reports only the sign of the input. It is one for positive numbers, minus one for negative numbers and zero at zero. The graph is two horizontal rays with a single point at the origin, so the range has just three values.

slides.heading: The greatest integer function
slides.body_md: $[x]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$: $[x] = n$ for $n \le x < n + 1$.

visual.alt: Graph of the greatest integer function: a staircase of flat steps, each starting at an integer with a solid left end and ending just before the next integer. The steps at heights minus 2, minus 1, 0, 1 and 2 are shown, with solid points at (minus 1, minus 1), (1, 1) and (2, 2).
visual.caption: Each step is $1$ wide and $1$ higher than the one before.

slides.narration: The greatest integer function rounds down. Every number from an integer up to, but not including, the next integer gives the same value, so the graph is a staircase. Each step starts with a solid dot at an integer. Negative numbers also round down, so the value at minus point five is minus one, not zero. The range is the set of all integers.

slides.heading: Quick check: rounding down
slides.body_md: Compare the greatest integer values of two nearby numbers.
slides.narration: Find the integer interval that each number lies in.

slides.heading: Exponential and logarithmic functions
slides.body_md: $a^x > 0$ for all $x$; $\log_a x$ needs $x > 0$. Their graphs are mirror images in $y = x$.

visual.alt: Graphs of y equal to 2 to the power x, through (0, 1), (1, 2) and (3, 8), and y equal to log base 2 of x, through (1, 0), (2, 1) and (8, 3). The two curves are mirror images of each other in the line y equal to x.
visual.caption: The coordinates swap: $(1, 2)$ on $2^x$ matches $(2, 1)$ on $\log_2 x$.

slides.narration: The exponential with base two passes through zero, one and always stays above the horizontal axis. The logarithm with base two is its mirror image in the line y equals x, so it passes through one, zero and exists only for positive inputs. Their coordinates swap: one, two on the first curve matches two, one on the second.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: sketching with the modulus
slides.body_md: Sketch $y = 3 - |x + 1|$ and read off its highest point, intercepts and range.

visual.alt: Graph of y equal to 3 minus mod of x plus 1: an upside-down V with its top at (minus 1, 3), crossing the x-axis at minus 4 and 2 and the y-axis at 2.
visual.caption: Highest point $(-1, 3)$; $x$-intercepts $-4$ and $2$; $y$-intercept $2$.

slides.narration: The modulus of x plus one is never negative, so three minus that is at most three, and the top is at x equals minus one. The graph crosses the horizontal axis where the modulus equals three, at minus four and at two. At x equal to zero the value is two. So the graph is an upside-down V and the range is every value up to three.

slides.heading: Quick check: floor value
slides.body_md: Evaluate the greatest integer function at a negative number.
slides.narration: Remember that the greatest integer function rounds down, towards negative numbers.

slides.heading: Algebra of real functions
slides.body_md: The sum, difference and product live on $D_f \cap D_g$. The quotient also needs $g(x) \ne 0$.

visual.alt: Table of the algebra of real functions: the sum, difference and product are defined on the common domain of f and g, and the quotient also removes the points where g is zero.
visual.caption: The quotient has one extra condition.

slides.narration: Two real functions combine pointwise. The sum, the difference and the product use the rule on every input where both functions are defined, the common domain. The quotient needs one more condition: the function in the denominator must not be zero. Always write the domain together with the new rule.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: four combinations
slides.body_md: For $f(x) = \sqrt{6 - x}$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 4$ find $f + g$, $f - g$, $fg$ and $\dfrac{f}{g}$ with their domains.
bullets: $g(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 2$, so the quotient excludes $-2$ and $2$

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: for f of x equal to the square root of 6 minus x and g of x equal to x squared minus 4, the sum, difference and product are defined for x up to 6, and the quotient also excludes minus 2 and 2.
visual.caption: $g(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 2$, so the quotient loses those two points.

slides.narration: The first function needs x at most six; the second works for every real number. Their common domain is every x up to six. The sum, the difference and the product use that domain. For the quotient, the denominator is zero at minus two and at two, so those two numbers are removed as well.

slides.heading: Quick check: where a quotient fails
slides.body_md: Decide when a quotient is defined on the whole common domain.
slides.narration: Look for a point where both functions exist but the divisor is zero.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Domain: exclude zero denominators, negative roots, non-positive logarithm arguments
Know the graph, domain and range of each standard function
Quotient: remove the zeros of the divisor too

nodes.label: Domain: exclude what breaks the rule

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: find the domain by excluding what breaks the rule, find the range by solving y equal to f of x for x, know the standard graphs, and for a quotient also exclude the zeros of the divisor.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Find a domain by excluding what breaks the rule. Find a range by solving for x. Know the standard graphs, especially the modulus, signum and greatest integer. When you divide functions, remove the zeros of the divisor from the common domain.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give the final domain in set or interval form
Check the end points of intervals separately
A quotient loses the zeros of the divisor

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: each rule 1, domains with the extra condition 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: domain questions award a mark per condition, domain and range questions award the domain, the solving step and the range, sketches award shape and key points, and algebra questions award each rule and the domain with the extra condition for the quotient.
visual.caption: State the final domain and range in interval or set form.

slides.narration: In the examination, write the final domain and range in interval or set form. Check each end point separately, because a root allows zero but a denominator does not. Remember that the greatest integer function rounds down, including for negative numbers. And for a quotient, never forget the zeros of the divisor.

notes.title: Relations and Functions - chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Ordered pairs and the Cartesian product
sections.body_md:
An **ordered pair** $(a, b)$ keeps its entries in order: $(a, b) = (c, d)$ exactly when $a = c$ and $b = d$.

The **Cartesian product** of $A$ and $B$ is $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$. In general $A \times B \ne B \times A$. With the reals, $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is the coordinate plane and $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is three-dimensional space. For finite sets, $A \times B = \varnothing$ when either set is empty.

key_terms.definition_md: Two entries in a fixed order; equal pairs agree entry by entry.
All ordered pairs with first entry from $A$ and second from $B$.

formulas.latex: A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}
formulas.label: Cartesian product

visual.alt: Grid for the product of A equal to the set 1, 2, 3 and B equal to the set p, q: the six ordered pairs (1, p), (1, q), (2, p), (2, q), (3, p), (3, q), one in each row and column cell.
visual.caption: Rows run over $A$, columns over $B$: $3 \times 2 = 6$ pairs.

visuals.alt: Coordinate plane with the line y equals x. The points (2, 4) and (4, 2) are mirror images in this line, so they are two different points, just as the ordered pairs are different.
visuals.caption: $(2, 4) \ne (4, 2)$: swapping the entries moves the point.

sections.heading: 2. Counting pairs and relations
sections.body_md:
If $n(A) = p$, $n(B) = q$ and $n(C) = s$, then $n(A \times B) = pq$ and $n(A \times B \times C) = pqs$.

A relation from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$, so the number of relations is $2^{pq}$ (the empty relation and the whole product included). Conditions such as "contains these $k$ pairs" reduce the count to $2^{pq - k}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A product with $pq$ pairs has $2^{pq}$ subsets, each a relation.

visual.alt: Counting table: for set sizes 2 and 3 the product has 6 pairs and there are 64 relations; for 3 and 3 there are 9 pairs and 512 relations; for 4 and 5 there are 20 pairs and 1048576 relations.
visual.caption: Pairs multiply; relations are subsets of the pairs, so they count as $2^{pq}$.

sections.heading: 3. Relations: arrow diagrams, domain, co-domain, range
sections.body_md:
A **relation** $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A \times B$; we write $x\,R\,y$ for $(x, y) \in R$. It can be given by a list of pairs, by a rule, or by an arrow diagram.

- **Domain:** the first entries that occur.
- **Co-domain:** the whole set $B$.
- **Range:** the second entries that occur, a subset of the co-domain.

Elements of $A$ with no arrow are not in the domain.

key_terms.definition_md: Set of first entries of the pairs of $R$.
The set $B$ in which the second entries must lie.
Set of second entries actually reached.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from A equal to 1, 2, 3, 4 to B equal to 0, 3, 8, 10, 15: the arrows go 1 to 0, 2 to 3, 3 to 8 and 4 to 15, so 10 receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $y = x^2 - 1$: domain $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, range $\{0, 3, 8, 15\}$, co-domain all of $B$.

visuals.alt: Arrow diagram of the relation x plus y equal to 7 from A equal to 1 to 6 to B equal to 2 to 5: 2 goes to 5, 3 goes to 4, 4 goes to 3 and 5 goes to 2, while 1 and 6 have no arrow.
visuals.caption: Elements $1$ and $6$ of $A$ have no partner, so they are outside the domain.

sections.heading: 4. Functions as special relations
sections.body_md:
A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a **function** when **every** element of $A$ has **exactly one** image in $B$; we write $y = f(x)$ and $f : A \to B$.

Two failures: an element of $A$ with no image, or with two images. Two elements may share an image, and the range may be smaller than the co-domain. To show a relation is not a function, name the offending element.

key_terms.definition_md: A relation in which each element of the domain set has exactly one image.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a function from X equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1, 2 to Y equal to 1, 4, 9: each element of X has exactly one arrow, minus 2 and 2 both go to 4, minus 1 and 1 both go to 1, and 9 receives none.
visual.caption: One arrow from every element of $X$; two elements may share an image.

visuals.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation that is not a function: from X equal to 1, 2, 3 to Y equal to 4, 5, 6, the element 1 has two arrows, to 4 and to 5, and the element 3 has no arrow at all.
visuals.caption: $1$ has two images and $3$ has none: not a function.

sections.heading: 5. Domain and range of real functions
sections.body_md:
For a real function given by a formula, the **domain** is the largest set of real numbers where the formula is a real number: avoid zero denominators, negative quantities under even roots and non-positive arguments of logarithms.

To find the **range**, put $y = f(x)$ and solve for $x$; a value $y$ is in the range when a real $x$ in the domain exists. For quadratics, completing the square shows the least or greatest value; for $\sqrt{\ }$ and $|\ |$, a non-negative quantity gives a bound at once.

key_terms.definition_md: A function whose domain and range are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.

visual.alt: Table of domain rules for real functions: a fraction needs a non-zero denominator, an even root needs a non-negative quantity, a root in a denominator needs a positive quantity, and a logarithm needs a positive argument.
visual.caption: Test each part of the rule, then combine the conditions.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equal to 3 minus 2x over x plus 4: two branches either side of the vertical line x equal to minus 4. The right branch crosses the x-axis at 1.5 and flattens towards the height minus 2; the left branch lies below minus 2.
visuals.caption: Solving for $x$ gives $x = \dfrac{3 - 4y}{y + 2}$: every $y$ except $-2$ is a value.

sections.heading: 6. Standard real functions and their graphs
sections.body_md:
Constant, identity, polynomial and rational functions are met early. The **modulus** $|x|$ has range $[0, \infty)$; the **signum** takes the values $-1$, $0$, $1$; the **greatest integer** $[x]$ rounds down and has range $\mathbb{Z}$ (so $[-1.01] = -2$); the **exponential** $a^x$ is always positive; the **logarithm** $\log_a x$ needs $x > 0$.

A graph transformed by shifting inside the modulus, such as $3 - |x + 1|$, keeps the V shape: find the tip, the intercepts and the range.

key_terms.definition_md: $[x]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$.

visual.alt: Table of the standard real functions with their domain and range: constant, identity, square, reciprocal, modulus, signum, greatest integer, exponential and logarithmic.
visual.caption: Learn the domain and range with each graph.

visuals.caption: Each step is $1$ wide and $1$ higher than the one before.

sections.heading: 7. Algebra of real functions
sections.body_md:
For real functions $f$ and $g$ with domains $D_f$ and $D_g$: $(f \pm g)(x) = f(x) \pm g(x)$ and $(fg)(x) = f(x)\,g(x)$ on $D_f \cap D_g$; $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ on $D_f \cap D_g$ with the zeros of $g$ removed.

Always state the domain with the new rule: the sum can exist at a point where the quotient does not.

key_terms.definition_md: The set $D_f \cap D_g$ where both functions are defined.

visual.alt: Table of the algebra of real functions: the sum, difference and product are defined on the common domain of f and g, and the quotient also removes the points where g is zero.
visual.caption: The quotient has one extra condition.

visuals.alt: Worked example 6 table: for f of x equal to the square root of 6 minus x and g of x equal to x squared minus 4, the sum, difference and product are defined for x up to 6, and the quotient also excludes minus 2 and 2.
visuals.caption: $g(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 2$, so the quotient loses those two points.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Listing a product or counting relations (2 marks):* the method or rule, then the list or number.
- *Relation from a rule (3 marks):* the pairs, then the domain and range.
- *Function or not (2-3 marks):* the test applied to each element, then the verdict with its reason.
- *Domain and range (3 marks):* each condition for the domain, the solving step, then the range.
- *Graphs (3 marks):* shape and key points, then the range.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $2^{p + q}$ instead of $2^{pq}$ for the number of relations.
- Confusing the range with the co-domain.
- Saying that two inputs sharing an output breaks the function rule.
- Rounding $[-1.01]$ to $-1$ instead of $-2$.
- Forgetting the zeros of $g$ when finding the domain of $\dfrac{f}{g}$.

cards.front_md: When are the ordered pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ equal?
cards.back_md: $a = c$ and $b = d$.

cards.front_md: Define the Cartesian product $A \times B$.
cards.back_md: The set of all ordered pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.

cards.front_md: Is $A \times B = B \times A$ in general?
cards.back_md: No, unless $A = B$ (or one of them is empty).

cards.front_md: How many elements does $A \times B$ have?
cards.back_md: $n(A \times B) = n(A) \cdot n(B)$.

cards.front_md: How many elements in $A \times B \times C$?
cards.back_md: $n(A)\,n(B)\,n(C)$, one choice for each entry.

cards.front_md: What is $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$?
cards.back_md: The set of all ordered pairs of real numbers: the coordinate plane.

cards.front_md: Define a relation from $A$ to $B$.
cards.back_md: Any subset of $A \times B$.

cards.front_md: How many relations are there from $A$ to $B$ if $n(A) = p$, $n(B) = q$?
cards.back_md: $2^{pq}$, one for each subset of $A \times B$.

cards.front_md: How many relations from $A$ to $B$ contain $k$ given pairs?
cards.back_md: $2^{pq - k}$: the other pairs are free.

cards.front_md: Domain of a relation
cards.back_md: The set of first entries of its pairs.

cards.front_md: Range of a relation
cards.back_md: The set of second entries of its pairs; a subset of the co-domain.

cards.front_md: Co-domain of a relation from $A$ to $B$
cards.back_md: The whole set $B$, used or not.

cards.front_md: What does an arrow diagram show?
cards.back_md: One arrow from $x$ to $y$ for every pair $(x, y)$ of the relation.

cards.front_md: Definition of a function from $A$ to $B$
cards.back_md: A relation in which every element of $A$ has exactly one image in $B$.

cards.front_md: Can two inputs of a function share an output?
cards.back_md: Yes. But one input may never have two outputs.

cards.front_md: Is a relation where some element of $A$ has no arrow a function?
cards.back_md: No: every element of $A$ needs an image.

cards.front_md: Domain of a real function from a formula
cards.back_md: The largest set of real numbers for which the formula gives a real value.

cards.front_md: Domain of $\dfrac{1}{x - 2}$
Domain and range of $\sqrt{9 - x^2}$
How do you find the range of $y = f(x)$?
cards.back_md: Solve for $x$ in terms of $y$; the range is the set of $y$ for which a real $x$ in the domain exists.

cards.front_md: Range of $|x|$
Values of $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$
Define $[x]$ and give its range.
cards.back_md: Greatest integer not exceeding $x$; range $\mathbb{Z}$. Example: $[-1.01] = -2$.

cards.front_md: What does the graph of $[x]$ look like?
cards.back_md: A staircase of unit steps; each step starts at an integer.

cards.front_md: Domain and range of $a^x$ ($a > 0$, $a \ne 1$)
cards.back_md: Domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$.

cards.front_md: Domain and range of $\log_a x$
cards.back_md: Domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$.

cards.front_md: Domain of $f + g$, $f - g$ and $fg$
cards.back_md: The common domain $D_f \cap D_g$.

cards.front_md: Domain of $\dfrac{f}{g}$
cards.back_md: $D_f \cap D_g$ with the points where $g(x) = 0$ removed.

cards.front_md: Common ISC mistake on counting relations
cards.back_md: Writing $2^{p + q}$ instead of $2^{pq}$.

cards.front_md: Example: $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = x - 1$. Where does $f + g$ exist but $\dfrac{f}{g}$ not?
cards.back_md: At $x = 1$: both are defined, but $g(1) = 0$.

questions.stem_md: Two ordered pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ are called equal exactly when
questions.solution_md: An ordered pair keeps its entries in position, so equality means the first entries agree **and** the second entries agree. Option (b) would make $(1, 2) = (2, 1)$.

questions.stem_md: Sets $A$ and $B$ have $7$ and $3$ elements respectively. The number of ordered pairs in $A \times B$ is
questions.solution_md: Each of the $7$ first entries pairs with each of the $3$ second entries, so $n(A \times B) = 7 \times 3 = 21$. Option (a) adds the sizes instead.

questions.stem_md: If $(2x - y,\ x + y) = (1,\ 8)$, the value of $xy$ is
questions.solution_md: Matching entries in position gives $2x - y = 1$ and $x + y = 8$. Adding, $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$ and $y = 5$, hence $xy = 15$. Swapping the two right-hand sides would give $x = 3$, $y = -2$ and the tempting $-6$.

questions.stem_md: Take $A = \{1, 3\}$ and $B = \{3, 6, 9\}$. Exactly one of the ordered pairs below lies in $B \times A$. Which one?
questions.solution_md: In $B \times A$ the first entry comes from $B$ and the second from $A$. Only $(9, 3)$ qualifies: $9 \in B$ and $3 \in A$. The pair $(1, 6)$ belongs to $A \times B$ instead.

questions.stem_md: The product $A \times B$ has $15$ elements and $n(A) = 3$. Then $n(B \times B)$ is
questions.solution_md: $n(B) = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5$, so $n(B \times B) = 5 \times 5 = 25$. Option (c) stops at $n(B)$ and (b) multiplies $15$ by $3$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{p, q, r\}$ and $C = \{u, v\}$. How many ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ lie in $A \times B \times C$?
questions.solution_md: Each triple is chosen in three independent steps with $2$, $3$ and $2$ possibilities: $2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12$. Option (d) forgets the set $C$; (a) adds the sizes.

questions.stem_md: A set $P$ has $2$ elements and a set $Q$ has $4$ elements. How many different relations from $P$ to $Q$ can be formed?
questions.solution_md: $P \times Q$ has $2 \times 4 = 8$ pairs and every subset of it is a relation, so there are $2^8 = 256$. The value $64$ comes from $2^{2 + 4}$, which mixes up addition and multiplication.

questions.stem_md: A relation $R$ from $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ to $\{3, 4, 5\}$ is defined by $x\,R\,y$ when $x + y$ is even. The number of ordered pairs in $R$ is
A relation is written $R = \{(2, 5), (3, 8), (2, 9), (7, 1)\}$. The domain of $R$ is
questions.solution_md: The domain collects the **first** entries, each listed once: $2, 3, 2, 7$ give $\{2, 3, 7\}$. Option (b) is the range and (c) mixes both.

questions.stem_md: $R$ is the relation from $X = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ to $Y = \{-1, 2, 5, 8, 11\}$ given by $y = 3x - 1$. Which element of $Y$ does **not** belong to the range of $R$?
questions.solution_md: The pairs are $(0, -1), (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8)$, so the range is $\{-1, 2, 5, 8\}$. The element $11$ would need $x = 4$, which is not in $X$.

questions.stem_md: $P = \{p_1, p_2\}$ and $Q = \{q_1, q_2, q_3\}$. How many relations from $P$ to $Q$ contain the pair $(p_1, q_1)$?
questions.solution_md: That pair is forced in; each of the other $6 - 1 = 5$ pairs of $P \times Q$ may be present or absent, giving $2^5 = 32$ relations. Option (a) is the count with no restriction.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one of these sets of ordered pairs, each a relation from $\{2, 4, 6\}$ to $\{1, 3\}$, defines a function. Which one?
questions.solution_md: A function must give each of $2, 4, 6$ exactly one partner. (b) leaves $6$ unused; (c) gives $2$ two partners; (a) gives $6$ two partners. In (d) all three share the image $3$, which is allowed.

questions.stem_md: The largest set of real numbers on which $f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 12}$ is defined is
questions.solution_md: A square root needs a non-negative inside: $3x + 12 \ge 0$ gives $x \ge -4$. At $x = -4$ the value is $\sqrt{0} = 0$, so the end point is included.

questions.stem_md: The real function $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2 - 5x + 6}$ is defined for every real $x$ except
questions.solution_md: Only a zero denominator is forbidden: $x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0$ at $x = 2$ and $x = 3$. A zero numerator at $x = 0$ simply gives the value $0$.

questions.stem_md: As $x$ takes every value for which it is defined, the function $f(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x - 1}$ takes exactly the values in
questions.solution_md: The domain is $x \ge 1$, and $\sqrt{x - 1} \ge 0$ with value $0$ at $x = 1$. So $f(x) \ge 2$, with $f(1) = 2$ reached. Every $y \ge 2$ occurs, using $x = (y - 2)^2 + 1$.

questions.stem_md: Taking every real $x$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2}$ is defined, the outputs $f(x)$ fill the set
questions.solution_md: Write $y = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2}$ and solve for $x$: $y(x - 2) = x + 1$ gives $x(y - 1) = 2y + 1$, so $x = \dfrac{2y + 1}{y - 1}$, possible exactly when $y \ne 1$. The excluded $2$ belongs to the domain, not the range.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^2}$, the set of all values that $f$ can take is
questions.solution_md: The domain is $[-3, 3]$ where $0 \le 9 - x^2 \le 9$, so $0 \le f(x) \le 3$, both ends reached (at $x = \pm 3$ and $x = 0$). A square root is never negative, which rules out (b).

questions.stem_md: Here $[x]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$. The value of $[-1.01] \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(-3) + |-5|$ is
questions.solution_md: $[-1.01] = -2$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(-3) = -1$, so the product is $2$; adding $|-5| = 5$ gives $7$. Truncating $[-1.01]$ to $-1$ gives the tempting $6$.

questions.stem_md: The highest point on the graph of $y = 2 - |x|$ is
questions.solution_md: $|x| \ge 0$, so $2 - |x| \le 2$ with equality only at $x = 0$. The graph is an inverted V with top $(0, 2)$; the points $(\pm 2, 0)$ are where it meets the $x$-axis.

questions.stem_md: The set of all values taken by the function $f(x) = [x] + [-x]$, with $[\cdot]$ the greatest integer function, is
questions.solution_md: If $x$ is an integer, $[x] + [-x] = x - x = 0$. If $x = n + t$ with $n$ an integer and $0 < t < 1$, then $[x] = n$ and $[-x] = -n - 1$, so the sum is $-1$. Hence the values are $-1$ and $0$.

questions.stem_md: Let $f(x) = x^2 - 2x$ and $g(x) = x + 5$. The value of the product function $(fg)(-2)$ is
questions.solution_md: $f(-2) = 4 + 4 = 8$ and $g(-2) = 3$, so $(fg)(-2) = 8 \times 3 = 24$. The sum gives $11$ and the difference gives $5$.

questions.stem_md: For the real functions $f(x) = \sqrt{5 - x}$ and $g(x) = x - 1$, the quotient function $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is defined on
questions.solution_md: The common domain is $(-\infty, 5]$ (where $f$ is defined; $g$ is defined everywhere). The quotient must also avoid $g(x) = 0$, that is $x = 1$. The end point $5$ stays, since $g(5) = 4 \ne 0$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $n(A) = 3$, then $n(A \times A) = 9$ and $n(A \times A \times A) = 27$.

**Reason (R):** For finite sets, $n(A \times B \times C) = n(A) \cdot n(B) \cdot n(C)$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: With $n(A) = 3$ the rule in R gives $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ for the triple product and $3 \times 3 = 9$ for two factors. R is true and is exactly the counting argument that makes A true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The range of $R = \{(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2)\}$, a relation from $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ to $B = \{2, 3, 4\}$, equals $B$.

**Reason (R):** The range of a relation is the set of second entries of its pairs.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: the second entries are $2, 3, 2$, so the range is $\{2, 3\}$. That makes A false, because $4 \in B$ is never a second entry. The range is a subset of $B$, not necessarily all of it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The range of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2}$ is the interval $(0, \infty)$.

**Reason (R):** The domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2}$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. R only lists the allowed inputs. A is true because $x^2 > 0$ makes $f(x) > 0$ and $x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}}$ gives every $y > 0$. Knowing the domain does not by itself explain the values, so R is not the explanation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For every real $x$, $|x| \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(x) = x$.

**Reason (R):** For every real $x$, $\operatorname{sgn}(x) = \dfrac{|x|}{x}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: for $x > 0$ the product is $x \cdot 1$, for $x < 0$ it is $(-x)(-1) = x$, and at $0$ both sides are $0$. R is false at $x = 0$, where $\dfrac{|x|}{x}$ is undefined but $\operatorname{sgn}(0) = 0$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The function $f(x) = 3^x$ never takes a value that is zero or negative.

**Reason (R):** A positive number raised to any real power is positive, so $3^x > 0$ for every real $x$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R states the reason directly: the base $3$ is positive, so every power $3^x$ is positive, whether $x$ is negative, zero or positive. That is why zero and negative values are never reached, which is A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For real functions $f$ and $g$, the quotient $\dfrac{f}{g}$ always has the same domain as the sum $f + g$.

**Reason (R):** The quotient $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is defined only where $g(x) \ne 0$, in addition to the common domain of $f$ and $g$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. Because of the extra condition $g(x) \ne 0$, the quotient can lose points that the sum keeps, so A is false. For $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = x - 1$, the sum is defined at $x = 1$ but the quotient is not.

questions.stem_md: The ordered pairs $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$ are equal only when $a = b$.
questions.solution_md: Equality needs $a = b$ (first entries) and $b = a$ (second entries). These agree exactly when $a = b$; for example $(2, 5) \ne (5, 2)$ but $(4, 4) = (4, 4)$.

questions.stem_md: If $A \times B$ has $12$ elements, then there are exactly $2^{12} = 4096$ different relations from $A$ to $B$.
questions.solution_md: Each relation is a subset of $A \times B$, and a set with $12$ elements has $2^{12} = 4096$ subsets (including the empty one).

questions.stem_md: A relation from $A$ to $B$ in which some element of $A$ appears as the first entry of no pair can still be a function from $A$ to $B$.
questions.solution_md: A function from $A$ must give **every** element of $A$ exactly one image. If some element of $A$ has no pair, it has no image, so the relation is not a function from $A$.

questions.stem_md: The values of $f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 5$ fill the interval $[4, \infty)$ exactly.
questions.solution_md: Completing the square, $f(x) = (x + 1)^2 + 4 \ge 4$, with $4$ reached at $x = -1$. For any $y \ge 4$, $x = -1 + \sqrt{y - 4}$ gives $f(x) = y$.

questions.stem_md: The greatest integer function gives the same value at $x = 2.3$ and at $x = 2.99$.
questions.solution_md: $[x] = 2$ for every $x$ with $2 \le x < 3$, and both $2.3$ and $2.99$ lie in that interval: $[2.3] = [2.99] = 2$.

questions.stem_md: For two real functions $f$ and $g$, the quotient $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is defined at every point of the common domain of $f$ and $g$.
questions.solution_md: It fails wherever $g(x) = 0$. For $f(x) = 1$ and $g(x) = x$, both are defined at $x = 0$, yet $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is not defined there.

questions.stem_md: If $n(A) = 4$, $n(B) = 5$ and $n(C) = 2$, the product $A \times B \times C$ contains exactly ____ ordered triples.
questions.solution_md: Choose the three entries independently: $4 \times 5 \times 2 = 40$.

questions.stem_md: The number of relations from a set with $3$ elements to a set with $1$ element is ____.
questions.solution_md: The product has $3 \times 1 = 3$ pairs and every subset is a relation: $2^3 = 8$.

questions.stem_md: The smallest **integer** at which $f(x) = \sqrt{2x - 9}$ is defined is ____.
questions.solution_md: The domain is $2x - 9 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge 4.5$. The smallest integer in $[4.5, \infty)$ is $5$.

questions.stem_md: Rounding down to an integer, the bracket $[-6.5]$ evaluates to ____.
questions.solution_md: The greatest integer not above $-6.5$ is $-7$, so $[-6.5] = -7$.

questions.stem_md: Over all real $x$, the largest value of the expression $7 - |x + 2|$ is ____.
questions.solution_md: $|x + 2| \ge 0$, and it is $0$ at $x = -2$. So the largest value is $7 - 0 = 7$.

questions.stem_md: With $f(x) = 2x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = x + 10$, the difference function $f - g$ equals ____ at $x = 3$.
Set $A$ holds the **distinct** letters of the word MATHEMATICS and set $B$ holds the **distinct** digits of the number $2026$. Find $n(A \times B)$.
questions.solution_md: $A = \{M, A, T, H, E, I, C, S\}$ has $8$ elements and $B = \{2, 0, 6\}$ has $3$. So $n(A \times B) = 8 \times 3 = 24$.

questions.stem_md: How many relations from $\{a, b\}$ to $\{1, 2, 3\}$ contain **both** the pairs $(a, 1)$ and $(b, 2)$?
questions.solution_md: Two of the $6$ pairs are forced in; each of the other $4$ may be present or absent: $2^4 = 16$.

questions.stem_md: For $x, y \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ let $R$ be the set of pairs $(x, y)$ for which $x - y$ is divisible by $3$. How many ordered pairs does $R$ contain?
questions.solution_md: The residues mod $3$ split the set into $\{1, 4\}$, $\{2, 5\}$, $\{3, 6\}$; pairs inside a block work, each block giving $2 \times 2 = 4$ pairs. So $|R| = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate $f(-3)$ for the real function $f(x) = \dfrac{3x - 1}{x + 2}$.
How many **integers** lie in the domain of $f(x) = \sqrt{40 - x^2}$?
questions.solution_md: The domain is $x^2 \le 40$, that is $|x| \le \sqrt{40} \approx 6.32$. The integers from $-6$ to $6$ number $13$.

questions.stem_md: If $f(x) = 3x^2 - 1$ and $g(x) = x - 3$, find the value of the quotient function $\dfrac{f}{g}$ at $x = 5$.
questions.solution_md: $f(5) = 74$ and $g(5) = 2 \ne 0$, so $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(5) = \dfrac{74}{2} = 37$.

questions.stem_md: Find the value of the sum $\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\right] + \left[\dfrac{2}{3}\right] + \left[\dfrac{3}{3}\right] + \dots + \left[\dfrac{10}{3}\right]$, where $[x]$ is the greatest integer function.
For a relation from a set $A$ to a set $B$, the set made of the second entries of its ordered pairs has the name
questions.solution_md: The first entries form the domain; the second entries that actually occur form the range. The co-domain is the whole target set, used or not.

questions.stem_md: Each function from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is, in particular, a relation from $A$ to $B$.
questions.solution_md: A function is a set of ordered pairs of $A \times B$, so it is a subset of $A \times B$. It is the special relation in which every element of $A$ occurs exactly once as a first entry.

questions.stem_md: The signum function takes the value ____ at $x = -9$.
questions.solution_md: For a negative number the signum is $-1$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(-9) = -1$.

questions.stem_md: The ordered pairs $(2x + y,\ x - y)$ and $(7,\ 2)$ are equal. Find $x$ and $y$.

answer.model_answer_md: Equal pairs have equal entries in the same positions, so $2x + y = 7$ and $x - y = 2$. Adding the two equations, $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$, and then $y = 3 - 2 = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Match entries, then solve the pair of equations.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \{2, 4\}$ and $B = \{1, 5, 9\}$, list the elements of $A \times B$ and state $n(B \times A)$. Do $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ share any ordered pair?

answer.model_answer_md: $A \times B = \{(2, 1), (2, 5), (2, 9), (4, 1), (4, 5), (4, 9)\}$ and $n(B \times A) = 3 \times 2 = 6$. A pair common to both would need both entries in $A \cap B$, but $A \cap B = \varnothing$, so they share **no** pair.

questions.solution_md: List row by row; a common pair needs entries from both sets.

questions.stem_md: The Cartesian product $A \times B$ equals $\{(3, p), (3, q), (5, p), (5, q)\}$. Find the sets $A$ and $B$, and write down $B \times A$.

answer.model_answer_md: First entries come from $A$, second entries from $B$: $A = \{3, 5\}$ and $B = \{p, q\}$. Swapping the order, $B \times A = \{(p, 3), (p, 5), (q, 3), (q, 5)\}$.

questions.solution_md: Read A from first entries and B from second entries.

questions.stem_md: A relation $R$ from $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ to $B = \{3, 5, 6, 8\}$ is defined by $x\,R\,y$ when $y - x$ is a prime number. Write $R$ in roster form.
questions.solution_md: Check differences x by x against the primes.

questions.stem_md: Let $R = \{(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 9), (5, 9)\}$ be a relation from $A = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 7\}$ to $B = \{4, 9, 16\}$. Write its domain and range, and say whether $R$ is a function from $A$ to $B$.

answer.model_answer_md: Domain $= \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ (first entries) and range $= \{4, 9\}$ (second entries). The element $7 \in A$ has no pair, so $R$ is **not** a function from $A$ to $B$.

questions.solution_md: Compare the domain with A.

marking_scheme.step: Not a function: $7$ has no image

questions.stem_md: Show that the relation $\{(x, y) : x, y \in \mathbb{R},\ |y| = x - 1\}$ is not a function from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

answer.model_answer_md: For $x = 4$ the equation becomes $|y| = 3$, which gives both $y = 3$ and $y = -3$. So $(4, 3)$ and $(4, -3)$ both belong to the relation: one input has two outputs. (Also, $x = 0$ gives $|y| = -1$, which has no solution.) Hence it is not a function.

questions.solution_md: One counter-example input with two outputs is enough.

questions.stem_md: Find the domain of the real function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x - 3}}$ and explain why $x = 3$ is excluded.

answer.model_answer_md: The square root needs $x - 3 \ge 0$, and the fraction needs $\sqrt{x - 3} \ne 0$. Together $x - 3 > 0$, so the domain is $(3, \infty)$. At $x = 3$ the denominator is $\sqrt{0} = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Both the root and the denominator impose a condition.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = 6x - x^2 - 5$, write $f(x)$ in the form $a - (x - h)^2$ to find its range, and find every $x$ with $f(x) = 4$.

answer.model_answer_md: $6x - x^2 - 5 = 4 - (x - 3)^2$. Since $(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$, $f(x) \le 4$, and every value below $4$ occurs, so the range is $(-\infty, 4]$. The value $4$ needs $(x - 3)^2 = 0$, so $x = 3$ only.

questions.solution_md: Complete the square, then read off the maximum.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the expression $|x| - [x]$ at $x = -2.5$, at $x = 0$ and at $x = 3.7$, reading the bracket as the floor of $x$.
questions.solution_md: Evaluate the modulus and the bracket separately.

questions.stem_md: The real functions $f(x) = x^2 - 1$ and $g(x) = 2x + 5$ are combined. Write the expressions for $(f + g)(x)$ and $(f - g)(x)$, and find $(fg)(2)$.
questions.solution_md: Combine the rules, then use the values at 2 for the product.

questions.stem_md: Ordered triples are equal when their entries agree in position. Find $x$, $y$ and $z$ if $(x + y,\ y + z,\ z + x) = (7,\ 9,\ 8)$.

answer.model_answer_md: The three equations are $x + y = 7$, $y + z = 9$, $z + x = 8$. Adding them, $2(x + y + z) = 24$, so $x + y + z = 12$. Subtracting each equation in turn gives $z = 12 - 7 = 5$, $x = 12 - 9 = 3$ and $y = 12 - 8 = 4$.

questions.solution_md: Add the three equations, then subtract each one from the total.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{2, 3, 4\}$. Find $(A \times B) \cap (B \times A)$ by listing, and show that it equals $(A \cap B) \times (A \cap B)$.

answer.model_answer_md: $A \times B$ has first entries in $A$, second in $B$; $B \times A$ the other way. A pair lies in both exactly when each entry belongs to $A$ and to $B$. Listing, $(A \times B) \cap (B \times A) = \{(2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2), (3, 3)\}$. Since $A \cap B = \{2, 3\}$, $(A \cap B) \times (A \cap B) = \{(2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2), (3, 3)\}$, the same four pairs.

questions.solution_md: A common pair needs both entries in A and in B.

questions.stem_md: A relation $R$ from $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ to $B = \{1, 4, 7, 8, 10\}$ is defined by $y = 3x - 2$. Write $R$ in roster form, give its domain and range, and name the element of $B$ left out of the range.

answer.model_answer_md: For $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$ the rule gives $y = 1, 4, 7, 10$, so $R = \{(1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 7), (4, 10)\}$. Domain $= \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and range $= \{1, 4, 7, 10\}$. The element $8$ of $B$ is not in the range.

questions.solution_md: Substitute each x, then compare the values with B.

questions.stem_md: $P$ has $2$ elements and $Q$ has $3$ elements. Find (i) $n(P \times Q)$, (ii) the number of relations from $P$ to $Q$, and (iii) the number of those relations that contain exactly $2$ ordered pairs.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $n(P \times Q) = 2 \times 3 = 6$. (ii) Every subset of $P \times Q$ is a relation: $2^6 = 64$. (iii) Choose which $2$ of the $6$ pairs are present: $\dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$.

questions.solution_md: Relations are subsets; exactly two pairs means choosing two of the six.

questions.stem_md: Each relation below is from $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ to $B = \{4, 5, 6\}$. Decide which are functions, with a reason in each case. $R_1 = \{(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4)\}$; $R_2 = \{(1, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 6)\}$; $R_3 = \{(x, y) : y = 7 - x\}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $R_1$ is a function: each of $1, 2, 3$ has exactly one image (the same image $4$ is allowed). $R_2$ is **not** a function: $1$ has two images, $4$ and $5$. $R_3 = \{(1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4)\}$ is a function: each element of $A$ has exactly one image.

questions.solution_md: List the pairs, then count the images of each element.

questions.stem_md: For the rational function $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 4}{2x - 5}$, determine where it is defined and which values it takes.

answer.model_answer_md: The denominator is $0$ at $x = \dfrac{5}{2}$, so the domain is $\mathbb{R} - \left\{\dfrac52\right\}$. Put $y = \dfrac{x + 4}{2x - 5}$: then $y(2x - 5) = x + 4$, so $x(2y - 1) = 5y + 4$ and $x = \dfrac{5y + 4}{2y - 1}$. This is possible exactly when $y \ne \dfrac12$, so the range is $\mathbb{R} - \left\{\dfrac12\right\}$.

questions.solution_md: Domain from the denominator; range by solving for x.

questions.stem_md: State the domain and the range of $g(x) = 3 + \sqrt{16 - x^2}$, justifying each.

answer.model_answer_md: $g$ is defined when $16 - x^2 \ge 0$, that is $-4 \le x \le 4$: domain $= [-4, 4]$. On this domain $0 \le 16 - x^2 \le 16$, so $0 \le \sqrt{16 - x^2} \le 4$, with $0$ at $x = \pm 4$ and $4$ at $x = 0$. Adding $3$, the values fill $[3, 7]$, so the range is $[3, 7]$.

questions.solution_md: Bound the root over the domain, then shift by 3.

questions.stem_md: Describe the graph of $f(x) = 4 - |x - 1|$: give its highest point, the $x$-intercepts, the $y$-intercept and the range.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $|x - 1| \ge 0$, $f(x) \le 4$ with $4$ reached at $x = 1$: the highest point is $(1, 4)$. $f(x) = 0$ means $|x - 1| = 4$, so $x = 5$ or $x = -3$. At $x = 0$, $f(0) = 4 - 1 = 3$. The range is $(-\infty, 4]$.

questions.solution_md: Treat it as an inverted V shifted right by 1 and up by 4.

questions.stem_md: Write the function $f(x) = [2x]$ on the interval $0 \le x < 2$ as a table of pieces, and give its range.

answer.model_answer_md: $[2x] = n$ when $n \le 2x < n + 1$, that is $\dfrac{n}{2} \le x < \dfrac{n + 1}{2}$. So $f(x) = 0$ for $0 \le x < \dfrac12$; $1$ for $\dfrac12 \le x < 1$; $2$ for $1 \le x < \dfrac32$; $3$ for $\dfrac32 \le x < 2$. The range is $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$.

questions.solution_md: Solve n ≤ 2x < n + 1 for each integer n.

questions.stem_md: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x - 3}$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 4}$. Find the domains of $f$, $g$, $f + g$ and $\dfrac{f}{g}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $f$ is defined for $x \ne 3$. $g$ needs $x^2 \ge 4$, so $x \le -2$ or $x \ge 2$. For $f + g$ take both: $(-\infty, -2] \cup [2, 3) \cup (3, \infty)$. For $\dfrac{f}{g}$ also drop $g(x) = 0$, that is $x = \pm 2$: $(-\infty, -2) \cup (2, 3) \cup (3, \infty)$.

questions.solution_md: Domains of f and g first, then intersect; for the quotient remove zeros of g.

questions.stem_md: With $f(x) = |x|$ and $g(x) = x$, write $f + g$ and $f - g$ without modulus signs for $x \ge 0$ and for $x < 0$, and find $\dfrac{f}{g}$ with its domain.

answer.model_answer_md: For $x \ge 0$, $|x| = x$, so $(f + g)(x) = 2x$ and $(f - g)(x) = 0$. For $x < 0$, $|x| = -x$, so $(f + g)(x) = 0$ and $(f - g)(x) = -2x$. The quotient $\dfrac{|x|}{x}$ is defined for $x \ne 0$: it is $1$ when $x > 0$ and $-1$ when $x < 0$; domain $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

questions.solution_md: Split at zero so the modulus can be removed.

questions.stem_md: State the domain and range of the exponential function $f(x) = 3^x - 2$ and of the logarithmic function $g(x) = \log_2 (x - 3)$.

answer.model_answer_md: $3^x$ is defined for all real $x$ and is always positive, taking every positive value; subtracting $2$ gives domain $\mathbb{R}$ and range $(-2, \infty)$. For $g$ we need $x - 3 > 0$, so the domain is $(3, \infty)$; and $\log_2 (x - 3)$ takes every real value (use $x = 3 + 2^y$), so the range is $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.solution_md: Exponentials are positive; logarithms need a positive argument.

questions.stem_md:
Let $A = \{2, 3, 5\}$ and $B = \{1, 4\}$.

(a) List the elements of $A \times B$ and state $n(B \times A)$. [2]

(b) The relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is given by $x\,R\,y$ when $x > y$. Write $R$ in roster form, find its domain and range, and decide with a reason whether $R$ is a function. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A \times B = \{(2, 1), (2, 4), (3, 1), (3, 4), (5, 1), (5, 4)\}$ and $n(B \times A) = 2 \times 3 = 6$.

(b) Test each pair of $A \times B$ for $x > y$: $(2, 1)$, $(3, 1)$, $(5, 1)$ and $(5, 4)$ pass; $(2, 4)$, $(3, 4)$ fail. So $R = \{(2, 1), (3, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4)\}$. Domain $= \{2, 3, 5\}$ and range $= \{1, 4\}$. $R$ is **not** a function, because the element $5$ has two images, $1$ and $4$.

questions.solution_md: List the product, filter by the rule, then count the images of each element.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Not a function: $5$ has two images

questions.stem_md:
A set $A$ has $3$ elements and a set $B$ has $2$ elements.

(a) Find $n(A \times B)$ and the number of relations from $A$ to $B$. [2]

(b) How many of these relations give every element of $A$ at least one partner in $B$? Of these, how many are functions from $A$ to $B$? [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n(A \times B) = 3 \times 2 = 6$, and each of the $6$ pairs is present or absent, so there are $2^6 = 64$ relations.

(b) For one element of $A$ the possible sets of partners in $B = \{u, v\}$ are $\{u\}$, $\{v\}$ and $\{u, v\}$: $3$ non-empty choices. The three elements choose independently, so there are $3^3 = 27$ such relations. A function allows only one partner each, $2$ choices per element, giving $2^3 = 8$ functions.

questions.solution_md: Count the choices per element of A, then multiply.

questions.stem_md:
Find the domain and the range of each real function.

(a) $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x - 2}$ [2]

(b) $g(x) = 2\sqrt{16 - x^2}$ [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The denominator vanishes at $x = 2$, so the domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{2\}$. Put $y = \dfrac{5}{x - 2}$; then $x = 2 + \dfrac{5}{y}$ exists for every $y \ne 0$, and $y = 0$ is impossible because $5 \ne 0$. The range is $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

(b) $16 - x^2 \ge 0$ gives $-4 \le x \le 4$: domain $[-4, 4]$. On it $0 \le 16 - x^2 \le 16$, so $0 \le \sqrt{16 - x^2} \le 4$ and $0 \le g(x) \le 8$, with $0$ at $x = \pm 4$ and $8$ at $x = 0$. Every value between occurs, so the range is $[0, 8]$.

questions.solution_md: Domain from the restriction; range by solving for x or bounding.

questions.stem_md:
Consider $f(x) = |x - 2| - |x + 1|$.

(a) Write $f(x)$ without modulus signs on $x < -1$, on $-1 \le x \le 2$ and on $x > 2$. [2]

(b) Hence find the range of $f$, and solve $f(x) = 0$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For $x < -1$: $|x - 2| = 2 - x$ and $|x + 1| = -x - 1$, so $f(x) = (2 - x) - (-x - 1) = 3$. For $-1 \le x \le 2$: $|x - 2| = 2 - x$ and $|x + 1| = x + 1$, so $f(x) = 1 - 2x$. For $x > 2$: $f(x) = (x - 2) - (x + 1) = -3$.

(b) On the middle piece $1 - 2x$ falls steadily from $3$ (at $x = -1$) to $-3$ (at $x = 2$), so every value from $-3$ to $3$ occurs, and the outer pieces give only $3$ and $-3$. The range is $[-3, 3]$. Solving $1 - 2x = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac12$, which lies in $[-1, 2]$, and the outer pieces never give $0$; so $x = \dfrac12$ only.

questions.solution_md: Remove the moduli interval by interval, then read the values off each piece.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Values of the middle piece from $3$ to $-3$

questions.stem_md:
An imaginary school library charges a fine of two rupees for every **completed** week of delay. For a delay of $d$ days with $0 \le d < 28$ the fine is $F(d) = 2\left[\dfrac{d}{7}\right]$ rupees, where $[\cdot]$ is the greatest integer function.

(a) Find the fine for delays of $6$, $7$, $20$ and $21$ days. [2]

(b) Write $F$ as a table of pieces, say at which values of $d$ the fine jumps, and give the range of $F$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $F(6) = 2[0.857\ldots] = 0$; $F(7) = 2[1] = 2$; $F(20) = 2[2.857\ldots] = 4$; $F(21) = 2[3] = 6$. So the fines are $0$, $2$, $4$ and $6$ rupees.

(b) $F(d) = 0$ for $0 \le d < 7$; $2$ for $7 \le d < 14$; $4$ for $14 \le d < 21$; $6$ for $21 \le d < 28$. The fine jumps at $d = 7, 14, 21$, where a week is completed. The range is $\{0, 2, 4, 6\}$.

questions.solution_md: Divide by 7 first, take the greatest integer, then double.

questions.stem_md:
Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$ and $g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 3}$.

(a) State the domain of $f$ and of $g$. [1]

(b) Find $f + g$ and $fg$, and their common domain. [2]

(c) Find $\dfrac{f}{g}$ with its domain, and evaluate it at $x = 8$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $f$ needs $x + 1 \ge 0$: domain $[-1, \infty)$. $g$ needs $x \ne 3$: domain $\mathbb{R} - \{3\}$.

(b) $(f + g)(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} + \dfrac{1}{x - 3}$ and $(fg)(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 1}}{x - 3}$, both on the common domain $[-1, \infty) - \{3\}$.

(c) $\dfrac{f}{g}(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}\,(x - 3)$. Since $g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 3}$ is never $0$, nothing more is removed: the domain is $[-1, \infty) - \{3\}$. At $x = 8$: $f(8) = 3$ and $g(8) = \dfrac15$, so $\dfrac{f}{g}(8) = \dfrac{3}{1/5} = 15$.

questions.solution_md: Intersect the domains; the quotient loses only zeros of g, and g has none.

questions.stem_md:
A school stall (imaginary) sells $x$ whole badges. The revenue is $R(x) = 40x$ rupees and the cost is $C(x) = 600 + 15x$ rupees.

(a) Find the profit function $P = R - C$ as an expression in $x$, and say what values $x$ can take. [2]

(b) Find the number of badges at which the stall breaks even. [1]

(c) Find the function $\dfrac{R}{C}$, and evaluate it at $x = 60$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $P(x) = R(x) - C(x) = 40x - (600 + 15x) = 25x - 600$ rupees, for $x = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ (whole numbers of badges).

(b) Break-even means $P(x) = 0$: $25x = 600$, so $x = 24$ badges.

(c) $\dfrac{R}{C}(x) = \dfrac{40x}{600 + 15x}$, defined for every $x \ge 0$ since $C(x) \ge 600 > 0$. At $x = 60$: $\dfrac{2400}{600 + 900} = \dfrac{2400}{1500} = 1.6$, so revenue is $1.6$ times the cost.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the rules for profit; divide them for the ratio.
